items.a10-h: The Pamir Disaster – the Worst in the History of Mountaineering: The Role and Contribution of the Israeli Team in the Search for the Missing*
items.a10-p002: On 13 July 1990 the greatest disaster in the history of mountaineering took place. Some fifty climbers who had gathered for an international event lost their lives in it, among them four Israelis, members of the Israeli Alpine Club: Benny Agur, Dov Mali, Gabi Manovla and Yuki Pereg, of blessed memory. The disaster struck at night: an earthquake brought down great blocks of ice, "seracs", and set off avalanches onto the tents pitched in a small valley known as "the Frying Pan", at an altitude of 3,005 metres, where the climbers were camped on their way to the summit of Lenin Peak (7,200 metres) in the Pamir range. This range is the highest in the former Soviet Union, and it forms the border between the Islamic republics of Tajikistan to the south and Kyrgyzstan to the north. The search went on for 26 days, until the authorities decided that it had been exhausted.
items.a10-src1: *Part of this article appeared in "Masa Acher" on 15 September 2008 (with thanks to Moshe Gilad).
items.a10-p003: Professor Agursky, Benny Agur's father and a Sovietologist with connections in Israel and in the Soviet Union, came across a muted report of the disaster in the Soviet press. Together with the other families he launched a vigorous fundraising drive to pay for a rescue expedition, and turned to the "Israeli Alpine Club"† (see the article "Return to the Place You Came From") to get it organized. He demanded of the Foreign Ministry – and was granted – that it act at the diplomatic level so that the expedition could reach the disaster area. Although the tragedy was an international one, the Israeli search and rescue team was the only foreign team that came forward to help, and its contribution won high esteem from the media and the public of what was then the Soviet Union.
items.a10-p004: From the top of the crane in the date grove at Ein Gedi, at 42 degrees in the shade, I saw two men running towards me and signalling me to come down. They introduced themselves as Foreign Ministry people, told me about the disaster in the Pamirs and, since I was a missing-persons search officer with experience and qualifications on ice and snow, asked me to leave for the place at once; they would see to all the arrangements. I made it clear to them that this was no mission for one man, but for a skilled team, equipped with clothing and gear that could hardly be found in Israel. But the main thing was that eight years had passed since I had retired from snow and ice mountaineering, with a firm decision never to go back to it; and besides, <span epub:type="pagebreak" role="doc-pagebreak" id="pg-67" title="63"/>the date harvest was upon us – the most pressing and important season in the date business – and I did not even have a valid passport. Nor do I speak Russian, I added.
items.a10-p005: I was sure that would be the end of it, but they were men with a mission, and they asked me to have a list of equipment ready by six in the evening and to stay by the phone. In the evening they called and said that the next day a car would come to take me to choose gear from the store of an elite unit, which held everything needed for operations from the ocean floor to the summits of the Himalaya. As for the kibbutz and the dates, everything had already been approved, and later two Russian-speaking alpinists, members of the club, would join me: Bela I would meet at Ben Gurion Airport, and Dima was at that moment on a course in Chamonix (Mont Blanc), already acclimatized to altitude, and would join us in Zurich. I had run out of excuses, but not out of misgivings.
items.a10-p006: Just before take-off they brought me a new passport, and someone laid a big, heavy video camera in my lap, without understanding what the quick passage from the vineyards of Ein Gedi to the glaciers of the Pamirs means for the body. I decided that I would throw the camera into the first crevasse I met, without the slightest pang of conscience.
items.a10-p007: At our embassy in Moscow we learned that bribes in dollars and Marlboro cigarettes were the oil that would turn the wheels of the many strange means of transport we would need to reach the foot of the Pamir range – and this proved entirely true later on. We had to get to Dushanbe, the capital of Tajikistan, but at the airport for domestic flights they would not let us through without an outrageous payment in "greens". In Dushanbe we had enough time to make a first acquaintance with the typical faces of the people of Central Asia. The varied, fresh abundance in the markets was astonishing, next to the shameful poverty of what was on offer in Moscow.
items.a10-p008: The connecting flight, in a small plane, was to the town of Jirgatal – the last airstrip before the Pamir range. Every seat and every aisle was crammed with men and women with bundles of produce, and a few goats that they had not managed to sell in Dushanbe. I went straight to the indifferent pilot and waved our tickets, but he ignored me. When I pulled out two packs of Marlboro he showed some interest, and demanded a third. Then, with the help of the co-pilot, he packed the contents of the plane tighter, the human contents included, and cleared three seats to cries and bleats of protest.
items.a10-p009: The last part of the journey was in a passenger helicopter that crossed exceptionally high ridges. The view was wonderful, and below the snow line we could see flocks grazing on green slopes. Here and there smoke rose from a Kyrgyz yurt (a temporary summer dwelling). Whenever one of the passengers suffered from lack of oxygen, the flight engineer would press to his face a mask connected to an oxygen tank.
items.a10-p010: I did not know our missing men, and when we reached the base camp at Achik Tash (3,600 m), Boris took us to their tent. From video cassettes of their preparations in the Caucasus, which fitted the camera we had brought, I got some idea of their looks, their personalities and the social dynamics between them. (A link to the video is at the end of the article.)
items.a10-p012: Boris, a Jewish intellectual and a member of the Leningrad Alpine Club, had visited Israel shortly before the disaster and brought the Israeli club the news of the coming Pamir event. Benny, Dov, Gadi and Yuki, of blessed memory, "caught fire" and decided to take part. The experienced Boris took them under his wing, including days of training and acclimatization in the high Caucasus. After the tents were pitched in the valley of the Frying Pan, he went down to the lower camp for some errand, and when he came back up to the Frying Pan in the morning,
items.a10-p013: he was stunned to find it empty of tents and people. Boris is the tragic hero of this event, in which he lost 23 of his fellow club members, his partner among them, and the Israelis who were under his wing. He was also almost the only source of reliable information about the disaster, which he passed on to me in a detailed debriefing during the domestic flights from Moscow to the
items.a10-p016: Our main task for the next day was to adapt to the thin air. We knew that the quickest and most effective way to do it was to climb to the next camp (4,400 m) and come back down, and that is what we agreed to do. With difficulty and much suffering we reached the next camp and dropped to the ground exhausted, gripped by nausea and headaches. My companions did not keep to what we had agreed and refused to go down "only to come up again tomorrow". They knew very well that this was what had to be done, but they could not take it to heart. I forced the descent on myself, in the hope that they would follow me, but they held to their refusal. So I went down alone, and the next day I climbed up again, this time with relative ease. I found my companions still suffering from altitude sickness, and I decided to go on to the disaster site, to get to know the searchers and join them. After another day and night my companions recovered and joined as well.
items.a10-p017: I wanted to coordinate our work so that we would not repeat what had been done before us, but we found no leader there. Everyone did his best, but without any orderly plan. Moreover, the volunteers changed all the time, and no information, records or documentation passed between them. We heard that on the first day of the search two injured survivors and three bodies had been found and that the rest were still counted as missing, and someone also told me that a shoe with Hebrew letters had been found, but the man who found it was no longer there, and nobody knew where the shoe was, or where and when it had been found. Of course I was disappointed by the absence of the basic rules of searching for missing persons, and I said so, gently and with hesitation. My remarks were received willingly, even with appreciation, and I was promised that from then on they would be followed.
items.a10-p018: The first camp served as a secondary logistics base, and a helicopter brought equipment and volunteers up to it from base camp, as well as two large cartons we had brought from Israel. The camp was run by Yuri, a retired alpinist, who passed messages by radio between base camp and the Frying Pan. A large tent served there as dining room and kitchen, and in it some of the partners of the missing men laboured to scrape mould and rot off the provisions meant for the evening meals of the volunteers who came down from the Frying Pan.
items.a10-p019: Our cartons held mostly a surprising kind of emergency food, from the stores of the unit mentioned above: chiefly powders in thin packets, which with water and a short boil swell up and turn into mashed potato and soups that are tasty, nourishing and filling, and also a large quantity of small, dry salami sausages. To these the families at home had added piles of chocolate and treats of every kind, and also Ultrasol sun cream and lip balm of a quality far above what the volunteers had improvised.
items.a10-p020: One day we announced that this time we would make the meal. We came down from the Frying Pan a little early, lowered the rolled-up sides of the tent, prepared a feast fit for a king, and when the volunteers arrived we uncovered the laid tables. The amazement was great. One of the women said that nothing about the Israelis surprised her any more – we were riding the ripples of the worldwide admiration that the Home Front Command delegation had rightly won for its work after an earthquake in Turkey some time before – and after a peek into the rubbish bins she added: "All the same, it is a wonder where all the peelings went."
items.a10-p021: As "head of the Israeli team", I was called to a coordination meeting at base camp with the "heads of the rescue teams" of the Islamic republics that share the mountain between them. I was surprised; I knew nothing about them, and I had not seen them on the mountain. Down below it became clear to me that they were a kind of clerk, whose business was lists of equipment and volunteers. I found them sitting around a bottle of drink with their radio operators; the Kyrgyz (who is a Russian) sipped from a mug, while his radio operator was already filling the mug he held in his other hand. According to Boris, the bottle stayed full thanks to the radio operator, who siphoned off alcohol from the first-aid kits in the tents of the alpinists who had gone out onto the mountain.
items.a10-p022: The Tajik's radio operator, also a Russian (Sergei, from here on), knew a little English, and explained to me that I had been invited because an important newspaper correspondent had arrived "to cover the search". When the interview was over, I took the radio operator aside so that he could explain why the helicopter flew only to the first camp and did not come up to the Frying Pan. His answer was that the air there was too thin to allow it. I thanked him, sealed the new friendship with a pack of Marlboro, and hurried to the helicopter that was taking volunteers back to Jirgatal, for a briefing with Professor Agursky. The professor was a genius at human relations no less than he was a Sovietologist, and there he enjoyed the generous hospitality of a local family, and a line to Israel and the world through a radio amateur. I came back to Sergei with the news that the helicopter data I had sent to Israel allowed a landing at the Frying Pan, and gave him three bags, each holding a pack of Marlboro, salami and "Egozi" chocolate bars, for him and for the helicopter crew. The bags did their work until the end of the operation on the mountain!
items.a10-p023: I understood nothing of the interview. Back in Israel I was able to read it in a Hebrew translation made by my father-in-law, a former cultural attaché at the embassy in Moscow, who still followed the Soviet press. What the interview said was utterly absurd, but the coincidence was interesting.
items.a10-p024: The helicopter landings at the Frying Pan made it much easier to move volunteers and equipment, and it is a great pity that it had not occurred to me to act on the matter earlier. Towards the last week of the search we received important reinforcements, four more members of our club: Shai, Alon, Danny <span epub:type="pagebreak" role="doc-pagebreak" id="pg-72" title="68"/>and Doron. August was approaching, a month prone to avalanches; and most of all I feared the moment when the support of the local authorities would stop. I decided, with my companions' agreement, that we would stay the nights at the Frying Pan and so gain hours of daylight for work. We did not allow ourselves to sleep on the comfortable valley floor, for fear of the "seracs" (the ice blocks), although sleeping on the slopes was very uncomfortable, to put it mildly.
items.a10-p025: Groups of climbers kept arriving, among them groups from countries that had lost people in the disaster; not one agreed to help us with the work, except an American expedition, whose members agreed to stay a few hours. Nor did any expedition give up sleeping on the comfortable floor of the Frying Pan, despite our warnings. On sunny days, and most days were sunny, the heat in the Frying Pan rose very high, because of the radiation thrown back by the snow and the glaciers all around – hence its name.
items.a10-p026: The Frying Pan site was searched thoroughly by various means, and trenches were cut in the snow and the ice, but nothing was found. This small valley slopes down to a steep glacier split by many deep crevasses. Near its edge a number of objects and pieces of clothing came to light, and lower down, among the crevasses, more objects were found. It seemed, then, that the camp had not been buried by the avalanche where it stood, but swept onto the steep glacier, and that the people in it, with most of their gear, had been carried into the deep crevasses.
items.a10-p027: No one knew how deep the crevasses were. "Those in the know" said that some of them were surely 50 to 100 metres deep, and perhaps more. To check these crevasses was to risk lives. The blocks of ice around them were unstable, and at their mouths, hanging upon nothing, were icicles as sharp as spears, which threatened to fall on anyone going down inside and pierce his helmet, and him. I had to use my authority to forbid my companions to go near them. Even if the icicles did not break off of their own accord, the safety rope that must trail behind anyone who dares to go down could make them fall.
items.a10-p028: Even so, a few of the bravest and most skilled of the Russian alpinists went down to check some of the crevasses. They looked in and hurried back. After they had crossed themselves and thanked God for coming out safely – all of them, of course, confirmed atheists – they reported that checking the crevasses, besides being extremely dangerous, could never be completed anyway, because blocks of snow and ice from the avalanche, and the snow that had fallen since, had made partial plugs that barred the way and hid the bottom.
items.a10-p029: A few volunteers stayed with us at the Frying Pan at night as well, and together we huddled by one of our tents, which became the social and culinary centre, until the falling temperatures drove us into our sleeping bags. The failure to find the missing by the usual means made room for irrational methods, such as a "lucky rooster" that did no good and ended up in the cooking pot, a dog that stopped working after a short time because of snow glare, and a parapsychologist (see "A Friend from Another World" in this book) who believed that powers granted to him from beyond the Earth protected him from altitude sickness and made acclimatization unnecessary.
items.a10-p030: The search for survivors went on, as I said, for 26 days, until the logistical support was taken from us – mainly the helicopter, which had been almost entirely at our disposal. Many dozens of highly experienced Russian alpinists took part, most of them from the Leningrad club (today Leningrad has gone back to its original name, Saint Petersburg), and we, seven Israelis, in an expedition sent by the families and the Israeli Alpine Club.
items.a10-p031: To accept that there was no chance of reaching the missing, although we knew with high probability where they were, was hard. No wonder, then, that it was hard to tear ourselves away from the mountain and from those buried in it, and the last days of the search were driven by feeling and not by reason.
items.a10-p033: Statistics show that the Pamir range claims victims every year among those who climb its slopes. True, experience, skill and judgement raise the chances of survival, but blind avalanches like this one, which make no distinction between a novice and a grand master, are not rare. The more experienced alpinists are, the better they know that in the end their survival is a matter of probability.
items.a10-p034: Two questions come back after every disaster. One is specific: could it have been prevented? The other is more general: why do people take risks when there is no existential need? In the conquest of glaciers and snowy summits, as in other activities with an adventurous motive, the two questions are bound up with each other, and their root lies in human nature. Risk means a chance of disaster, and the essence of adventure is to face that chance. For this reason the next question, whether the risks of adventure can be reduced, does not seem relevant, since a survival instinct is rooted in every person, and adventurers are not suicidal. Because the forces of nature cannot be restrained, it may be better to strengthen the survival instinct of climbers through information and education. If this succeeds, the survival instinct will work to persuade its owner to prepare himself as well as he can for the unequal contest with the forces of nature, which may take him by surprise when he bursts onto their home ground.
items.a10-p035: Veterans of adventure, who became aware of the survival instinct in the course of their adventures, naturally seek to perfect their ability to survive through training, the right equipment, curbing their rashness and better judgement. Others go further and give up from the start the situations in which they may find themselves at a disadvantage against the forces of nature. They turn, for example, to rock climbing below the snow line. More exposed to risk are "the unaware", that is, the inexperienced, whose survival instinct has not yet had to raise an outcry. More exposed still are "those who do not want to know", the "it'll be fine" people. Some of them have lost their lives on glaciers in the past, shod in sandals and dressed in shorts. Such people can sometimes be met at an earlier stage, abseiling in the canyons of the Judean Desert, in calm and unthreatening surroundings, happy and good-hearted at having saved themselves the price of lessons. Most of them stay happy and good-hearted at least until the next gamble.
items.a10-p036: There is also a minority who, out of self-deception, obey the urge for adventure as if they were fulfilling a religious commandment. Its members perhaps quote "Arise, walk through the land" and are careful to say the "Wayfarer's Prayer", but fail at "Take ye therefore good heed unto yourselves", and scorn, or know nothing of, the means of navigation and the amount of water that is needed.
items.a10-p037: Veterans of adventure become aware, as I said, of the survival instinct, and they must decide whether to perfect their ability to survive before the next adventure or to avoid it. A fierce snowstorm that caught me in 1982, somewhere in the French Alps, made me decide to give up the situations in which I might find myself at a disadvantage against the forces of nature. My main hobby since then has been rock climbing. I love to flow with the rock, and I do not think of it in terms of conquest. The forces of nature do not plot against me, and it depends on me alone whether anything happens to me on the cliff. I feel no need or wish to contend with my surroundings, but I have already had to take part, to my regret, in struggles to protect them from those who do not understand their value. And yet I must hold a paradox: I am very glad that I lived through those tremendous experiences on the glaciers and the snowy summits. And in the face of the Pamir disaster – I am glad that I stopped in time.
items.a10-p038: In the Pamirs we were exposed to a certain degree of danger in the valley where we worked, since masses of ice, "seracs" that had not yet fallen, still hung above it upon nothing, and there was no shortage of crevasses along our routes. It is also known that earthquakes come in series and could have started again, although the later ones are usually weaker than the first. One could argue, then, that we took on ourselves, in an adventurous way, risks for which there was no existential need. But what we were contending with was not the chance that a disaster would happen, which is the essence of adventure, but the slim chance of finding the missing.
items.a10-p039: My view of adventure is that the motive decides whether an act is adventurous or not. This view allows me, as a member of the Judean Desert rescue team, to leave the calm of rock climbing when needed and to help in searching for the missing. The aim here is to bring help to people who have fallen into distress, and at times this involves operations that are mistakenly seen as adventurous. Yet even in such situations, when the motive is not adventurous, one must not be carried beyond the limit set by the balance of risk against chance, which is shaped by the terrain, the means and the skill.
items.a10-p040: As head of the Israeli expedition to the Pamirs, I set that limit for us at the edge of the deep crevasses.
items.a10-p041: Because of global warming and the melting of the glaciers, in September 2008 remains of those who died in the disaster of July 1990 came to light at the Frying Pan, and they confirmed the conclusions of the search operation of that time. It is now possible to collect at least a large part of the remains, and DNA identification technology exists and is used successfully when it is needed.
items.a10-p042: Even so, mountaineering tradition chooses to leave the dead buried in the place that is "natural" to them, and to set up memorials to them nearby. We saw such memorials in the Pamirs when we first went up, and one more was added to them after we left. Even Professor Agursky supported this, in complete contrast to Jewish tradition, which firmly requires that everything possible be done to bring the fallen, or at least their remains, to a Jewish grave. Here too, in my humble opinion, one must not be carried beyond the limit set by the balance of risk against chance.
items.a10-p044: The heavy video camera with which I began the account of the journey to the Pamirs, and which was meant to be abandoned, received a "pardon" the moment I saw our missing men on its screen at the Pamir base camp. In the end, apart from what we filmed with it and the testimony I took down from Boris, it occurred to no one in the local establishment – the heads of the rescue teams – nor in the Leningrad club, which had lost 23 of its members, that any documentation was needed. But a firm friendship was formed between us, and they asked, really begged, that after some necessary business in Moscow we put off our return home by a week and come to Leningrad, to meet families of the dead and to show the material we had filmed. It was impossible to refuse them. And so the camera that I had met with hostility closed the journey to the Pamirs with an act full of compassion.
items.a10-p045: Those were the days of "glasnost" – the reforms and openness that Gorbachev introduced – and crowds of Jews thronged the gates of the embassy to get a visa to Israel. It was truly hard to force a way through to store the equipment before the trip to Leningrad.
items.a10-p046: In Leningrad "an acquaintance from the mountain" was waiting for us, with the news that the head of the television station (which had the highest ratings and credibility in the country) was impatient to interview me. He was well dressed and well tied, as befitted his cultural and social standing; and I was in a tracksuit and a T-shirt that stank of the sweat of the Frying Pan, with the logo of Metzoke Dragot – which had made people curious on the mountain because of its ibex figure – and with Dima as my interpreter.
items.a10-p047: We sat facing him. Beyond Dima's translation, it was not hard to read his warm and approving body language. I was tired and a little bored, and I pulled out of my pocket the Marlboro pack on duty, a tested means of making friends that had become a habit. A second later I thought it a mistake, given the standing of the head of the most important television station in the country, but the pack was already out and his eyes lit up. The next day we could not walk down the street: people recognized us and thanked us warmly, and cars stopped to take us wherever we wanted.
items.a10-p048: Later, after the gates had opened and Israel had launched the "First Home in the Homeland" programme, a few families of immigrants chose to settle in Ein Gedi because they had heard about it in that interview.
items.a10-p049: To sum up: our expedition had a significant influence on the search efforts, and it clearly raised Israel's prestige in Europe in general, and in the Soviet Union of the time in particular.
